title: Roman doctors — Scripture not given as sole rule; Bellarmine on Augustine
source_text: V. Sequitur jam ut exquiramus quae sit de hac quaestione Doctorum Ecclesiae Romanae sententia. Primo igitur docent, Scripturam non esse datam Ecclesiae in hunc finem, ut esset unica fidei regula, atque ut ex ea sola religionis instituta & fidei dogmata peti & erui deberent. Itaque non esse necesse, ut omnia quae pertinent ad fidem atque mores, ex Scriptura sacra probentur. Non negant tamen illa, quae ad salutem singulis simpliciter necessaria sunt, in Scriptura sacra reperiri, ut videre est apud Bellarminum, De verbo Dei lib. 4. cap. 11. §. ultimo. Ubi respondens ad illud Augustini quod a nostris pro sua sententia afferri solet, In his quae aperte posita sunt inquit, Scriptura inveniri illa omnia quae continent fidem moresque vivendi. Limitat, inquit, de illis dogmatibus quae necessaria sunt omnibus simpliciter, qualia sunt quae habentur in Symbolo Apostolico, & in Decalogo. Et in sequentibus probat illud ejusdem Augustini, Credo quod etiam hinc divinorum eloquiorum clarissima authoritas esset, si homo illud sine dispendio promissae salutis ignorare non posset.
pass_a_gloss: It follows now that we inquire what the opinion of the Doctors of the Roman Church is on this question. First, therefore, they teach that Scripture was not given to the Church for this end, that it should be the sole rule of faith, and that from it alone the institutes of religion and the dogmas of faith ought to be sought and drawn out. And so it is not necessary that all things which pertain to faith and morals be proved from sacred Scripture. Yet they do not deny that those things which are simply necessary to salvation for individuals are found in sacred Scripture, as may be seen in Bellarmine, De verbo Dei book 4, chapter 11, last paragraph. Where, answering that saying of Augustine which our side is accustomed to bring for its opinion — In those things which are openly set down, he says, in Scripture are found all those things which contain faith and the morals of living — he limits it, he says, to those dogmas which are necessary to all simply, such as are held in the Apostles Creed and in the Decalogue. And in what follows he proves that same Augustine: I believe that even from this the clearest authority of the divine oracles would exist, if a man could not be ignorant of that without loss of the promised salvation.
pass_b_english: We turn next to the Roman doctors on this question.

First they teach that Scripture was not given so the Church would have it as the sole rule of faith, or so that religion's institutes and the dogmas of faith would have to be sought from it alone. So not everything that belongs to faith and morals need be proved from sacred Scripture.

They do not deny that what is simply necessary to each person's salvation is found in Scripture — see Bellarmine, De verbo Dei 4.11 (last section). Answering Augustine's line our side cites (In what is openly set down in Scripture are found all things that contain faith and the way of life), he limits it to dogmas simply necessary for all, such as the Apostles' Creed and the Decalogue, and presses Augustine's further point about ignorance that would cost promised salvation.

choices.why: Paired with peti for seeking doctrine from the text.
